primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'disciple' (Greek mathētēs, 'learner') primarily signifies a committed follower of Jesus Christ — one who learns from him, obeys his teaching, imitates his life, denies self, takes up the cross, and is being formed into his likeness. It functions as the normative identity of every Christian: to be a Christian is to be a disciple, a lifelong apprentice of Jesus marked by obedience, love, and fruit-bearing.
primary_basis: Matthew 28:19-20 (the Great Commission: 'make disciples of all nations... teaching them to obey')
Luke 9:23 / Matthew 16:24 ('If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me')
Luke 14:26-27, 33 (the cost of discipleship: renouncing all to follow Jesus)
John 8:31-32 ('If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples')
John 13:34-35 ('By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another')
John 15:8 ('By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples')
Acts 11:26 ('the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch')
Matthew 10:24-25 ('a disciple is not above his teacher... it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher')

alternatives.meaning: Disciple as every believer/Christian without distinction: in Acts the word simply denotes members of the church (Acts 6:1-2, 7; 9:1, 26; 11:26), so 'disciple' is equivalent to 'Christian' rather than describing a special level of commitment.

Disciple in the restricted historical sense: primarily the Twelve (or a wider inner circle such as the Seventy) whom Jesus personally called, trained, and commissioned — a technical designation of Jesus' immediate companions rather than all believers.

Two-tier or 'discipleship as a higher calling' reading: a disciple is a believer who has gone on to costly commitment, so one can be saved without yet being a disciple. Associated with some Free Grace/dispensational teaching and popular discipleship literature; strongly contested by Lordship-salvation and most Reformed/Catholic teaching.
basis: Luke 14:25-33 (read as conditions beyond saving faith)
John 8:31 (read as 'truly' disciples vs. mere believers)

alternatives.meaning: Disciple as rabbinic apprentice/imitator: scholarly and Jewish-background readings stress that mathētēs mirrors the rabbi-talmid relationship — living with the teacher, memorizing and replicating his life — so discipleship symbolizes formation by imitation more than intellectual learning.
basis: Luke 6:40 ('everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher')
Mark 3:14 ('that they might be with him')

alternatives.meaning: Broader usage for followers of other teachers or movements: disciples of John the Baptist, of Moses, or of the Pharisees, showing the term itself is generic for 'adherent of a teacher' rather than uniquely Christian.

notes: 'Disciple' is less a symbol than a role designation, but its figurative/theological meaning is well settled: a learner-follower of Jesus whose life is defined by obedience, self-denial, imitation, love, and fruit-bearing. The main live disagreement is not over this core meaning but over scope — whether 'disciple' equals every believer (the majority view, grounded in Acts and the Great Commission) or names a costlier, optional level of commitment (a minority position in evangelical debate). Historical-critical scholarship also distinguishes the narrower Gospel usage (the Twelve and Jesus' immediate followers) from the church's later generalized usage.
